articles.title: Baba Miller vuelve a batir su tope anotador por segunda noche consecutiva
articles.standfirst: El español sumó 13 puntos con 4/4 en tiros de campo en otra dura derrota de los Clippers
articles.summary: El español sumó 13 puntos con 4/4 en tiros de campo en otra dura derrota de los Clippers
articles.body: Por segundo partido consecutivo, Baba Miller batió su tope de anotación en la NBA. El jugador español sumó 13 puntos sin fallo en tiros de campo (4/4, incluido en triple) en la amplia derrota frente a los Suns por 133-110. Pese a estar en un contexto complicado por la acumulación de derrotas (balance de 2-8), progresa adecuadamente. Su aprovechamiento de los minutos es de las pocas noticias positivas de la franquicia. En un partido de los Clippers con la anotación muy repartida, Miller fue el máximo anotador de su equipo, aunque todo lo que hizo fue con la noche ya resuelta, pues no salió hasta que restaban 3:39 para el final del tercer cuarto y el marcador estaba en 91-59. Luego lo jugó todo. A su estadística cuatro rebotes y un tapón en los 16 minutos que estuvo en pista. Mientras él jugó, su equipo ganó por nueve. Rui Hachimura y Darius Garland también llegaron a los 13 puntos y otros cuatro jugadores alcanzaron la decena Fue otra noche dolorosa para los Clippers, que no pudieron competir en Phoenix y, tras ganar el primer partido de la temporada, han perdido ocho de los nueve siguientes y aún no han conseguido ganar fuera de casa (0-5). Esta vez, el choque estaba resuelto al descanso, al que los Suns se llevaron 17 puntos de ventaja. A falta de cuatro minutos para el final del tercer cuarto, el marcador ya era de 91-59. Ahí fue cuando el entrenador Tyronn Lue decidió que era momento de sacar a Miller. Los angelinos están en plena reconstrucción tras un verano convulso por las sanciones de la NBA por el fraude de Kawhi Leonard, ahora de regreso a Toronto. El edificio debería comenzar por los sólidos cimientos de la defensa, pero está costando. Son el cuarto equipo del Oeste que más puntos encaja. Ante los Suns recibieron 22/43 triples. Ahí destacó Jordan Goodwin, que metió seis de sus siete lanzamientos saliendo del banquillo y en sólo 14 minutos. Acabó con 18 puntos, máximo anotador de los locales. Devin Booker llegó a los 17. Luke Kennard metió 14 con 3/5 desde el arco, Jalen Green sumó 13 con 3/4 y Collin Gillespie 12 con 4/9. Un recital triplista ante el que los Clippers no opusieron resistencia.

articles.title: "Nunca vi un campeón NBA en el que sus tres estrellas fueran blancas y no va a pasar este año"
articles.standfirst: El polémico analista Stephen A. Smith hace un vaticinio sobre los Lakers basado en la raza de sus tres principales figuras
articles.summary: El polémico analista Stephen A. Smith hace un vaticinio sobre los Lakers basado en la raza de sus tres principales figuras
articles.body: Como en los viejos tiempos, la jornada de la NBA ha dejado a los Celtics en lo alto de la Conferencia Este y a los Lakers al mando del Oeste. Los angelinos, con un balance de 10-2, son los líderes de la competición. Buenas sensaciones con un Luka Doncic de otro planeta (promedios de 39,3 puntos, 7,8 rebotes, 7,9 asistencias y 2,0 recuperaciones) pero quizás demasiado pronto para saber cuáles son las verdaderas aspiraciones del equipo. Sin embargo, hay quien ya tiene claro que no serán aspirantes al anillo. Y en su conclusión no recurre al juego ni al talento... sino a la raza. El polémico analista Stephen A. Smith asegura: "Nunca he visto a un equipo de la NBA con tres jugadores blancos como principales figuras ganar un campeonato. Nunca ha sucedido y les aseguro que no creo que vaya a suceder este año". El mencionado Doncic, Austin Reaves y el recién fichado Walker Kessler son las estrellas de los Lakers y ser caucásicos parece ser una tara en opinión de Smith. "Sé que es polémica, pero no creo que pasen de la segunda ronda. Me sorprendería mucho si lo hicieran", dice el analista, que por delante a los Thunder, a los Spurs e incluso a los Nuggets y cree que habría igualdad con los Rockets y los Timberwolves cuando se recupere Anthony Edwards. El discurso de Smith no niega lo evidente, el gran momento de Doncic: "Está imparable. Está dejando a todos boquiabiertos. Va a ser candidato a MVP. No hay duda de que es especial”. Considera que "los Lakers son un equipo de playoffs", pero una vez en las series por el título no les da muchas opciones: "Llegarán a la segunda ronda, sufrirán una derrota humillante y se irán a casa". El analista sí cree que en un futuro los Lakers puedan aspirar a cotas muy altas. "La nueva directiva está liderada por Kushner y Bob Iger. Bob Iger es, en mi opinión, el Michael Jordan del deporte. Es el mejor ejecutivo que he conocido, un mentor y un amigo. Creo que los Lakers están en buenas manos y el futuro se presenta increíblemente prometedor", sentenció.

articles.title: Stephen Curry calls out Gilbert Arenas, Nick Young and others for criticism of wife Ayesha's new movie
articles.summary: Gilbert Arenas and Nick Young were talking about Ayesha Curry's new movie, "Second Chance Holiday" on a recent podcast.
articles.body:
Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry took to social media on Wednesday to defend his wife, Ayesha, after she appeared in a new movie.

Curry posted a video to Instagram to address criticisms that were made of Ayesha's acting in the Roku movie, "Second Chance Holiday," which debuted last week. Curry even called out former NBA players Nick Young and Gilbert Arenas, and former NFL player Emmanuel Acho, directly.

"I've been hearing a lot of noise, and usually the noise doesn't bother me, doesn't bother Ayesha. But this one in particular, when you're trying to step on the accomplishments of my wife [bothers me]," Curry said.

Ayesha plays a dating expert that is "determined to break her so-called 'curse' of always getting dumped during the holiday season" in the new movie, via IMDB . The movie came out on Nov. 5 on Roku. This is just the latest project that Ayesha has appeared in over the years. She's been in several films, including "Irish Wish" and "Joy to the World," and in several shows like "Ballers," "Hannah Montana" and more. She and Stephen got married in 2011, and have three children together.

But a lot of the discourse about the new movie, at least from Young and Arenas on a podcast on Saturday, had to do with Ayesha's kissing scene in the movie. Arenas said on the podcast that "she doesn't act like the other superstars' wives," like Michael Jordan's wife or Magic Johnson's wife, and that they "want" the kissing scene to be problematic because "Steph is so innocent."

"[This is] something that kinda speaks to a bigger conversation on how you view women in this world and what they're allowed and what they're not allowed to do," Curry said. "Even the ignorance behind how acting works. Obviously, I tried to laugh this one off, but something needs to be said. "Anytime Ayesha Curry shows up in your headline, I'd kindly suggest you just give the happy hands, the congratulations, and maybe, just maybe, the apology can be as loud as y'all leading y'all's shows with this topic. "So, appreciate the free [publicity]. Thank you for giving a nice shoutout to 'Second Chance Holiday,' which y'all can find on Roku, starring Ayesha Curry."

"[This is] something that kinda speaks to a bigger conversation on how you view women in this world and what they're allowed and what they're not allowed to do," Curry said. "Even the ignorance behind how acting works. Obviously, I tried to laugh this one off, but something needs to be said.

"Anytime Ayesha Curry shows up in your headline, I'd kindly suggest you just give the happy hands, the congratulations, and maybe, just maybe, the apology can be as loud as y'all leading y'all's shows with this topic.

"So, appreciate the free [publicity]. Thank you for giving a nice shoutout to 'Second Chance Holiday,' which y'all can find on Roku, starring Ayesha Curry."

Arenas tried to explain his statements on a new podcast episode on Wednesday after Curry's video, and later apologized "if [Curry] is offended." Young apologized, too.

Curry is in his 18th season with the Warriors. He's averaged 30.6 points, 4.3 assists and 4.1 rebounds through nine games this season. The Warriors sit at 8-3 this season entering Wednesday night's matchup with the Houston Rockets.

articles.title: Lakers Extend Win Streak vs. Bucks, Box Score Stats, Highlights for Luka, Reaves, Kuzma, Top Players
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Lakers are still on fire.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Lakers are still on fire.

Despite losing Austin Reaves to a left heel injury in the third quarter, Los Angeles extended its winning streak to seven with a 123-112 victory over the Milwaukee Bucks on Wednesday at Fiserv Forum. It improved to 11-2, while the 1-11 Bucks continue to trend in the opposite direction with an eighth consecutive loss.

Prior to Reaves' injury, he and Luka Dončić were back in the lineup together against an overmatched Bucks squad after the former missed Monday's win over the Atlanta Hawks and the latter was sidelined for Sunday's win over the Detroit Pistons.

Dončić also had an injury scare in the fourth quarter, although the Lakers were well ahead and didn't need to risk anything by leaving him in the game:

The pairing played well prior to the setbacks, and Sandro Mamukelashvili picked up the scoring slack when needed.

While this was just one early season game, it was the type of matchup the Lakers could ill-afford to lose if they are going to remain a threat in the crowded race for the Western Conference's No. 1 seed.

Milwaukee is one of the worst teams in the league, and contenders such as the San Antonio Spurs, Minnesota Timberwolves, Houston Rockets and others will surely take care of business in their matchups. That means Los Angeles needs to do the same if it is going to keep pace.

Dončić and Reaves wasted no time setting the tone as the Purple and Gold built an 11-point halftime advantage. Dončić found his stroke from deep, while Reaves attacked the lane and took advantage of openings when the Bucks were too focused on No. 77.

He even mixed in a no-look basket and dunk in the first half for good measure before leaving in the third quarter.

It wasn't just the backcourt duo, though, as Mamukelashvili provided a spark off the bench with his outside shooting as the Lakers continued to seize control before Reaves exited.

It wasn't all bad news for the Bucks, as Nate Ament threw down a monster dunk while Tyler Herro took over for stretches with his scoring and facilitating. Jaime Jaquez Jr. also contributed off the bench, although the Lakers extended their advantage to 21 in the third quarter as Dončić found Walker Kessler by the rim before hitting Mamukelashvili and Ziaire Williams for triples.

By the time Dončić ended the quarter with an and-1 jumper, the game was all but secure for the visitors. That was notable, as there was no reason to consider putting Reaves back in the game following his injury with the Lakers cruising.

Whenever the Bucks built even the slightest bit of momentum, Dončić had an answer with either his shooting or willingness to create plays for others until his own night came to an end.

As a result, the Lakers still have plenty of momentum heading into Sunday's road game against the Phoenix Suns.

articles.title: Luka Doncic Injury Update, Latest on Lakers Star After Getting Hurt on Kyle Kuzma Foul
articles.summary: Los Angeles Lakers superstar Luka Dončić seemingly suffered an ankle injury at the end of his team's win over the Milwaukee Bucks:
articles.body:
Los Angeles Lakers superstar Luka Dončić seemingly suffered an ankle injury at the end of his team's win over the Milwaukee Bucks:

The guard landed on Kyle Kuzma while attempting a deep shot. Dončić was given a foul on the play and he took his free throw before exiting to the locker room.

After the game, Lakers coach JJ Redick downplayed the injury as a "tweak" and predicted Dončić will be "fine."

Dončić, 27, has been an absolute terror to open the 2026-27 season, averaging 39.3 points, 7.9 assists and 7.8 rebounds per game entering Wednesday. He added another 32 points against the Bucks before the injury.

He's largely been healthy, though he did miss a Nov. 8 game against the Detroit Pistons with lower-back tightness, the second game of the season he missed with that particular ailment.

The Lakers completely reshaped their roster around Dončić and Austin Reaves in the offseason, letting LeBron James walk in free agency while adding Walker Kessler, Ziaire Williams Sandro Mamukelashvili, Quentin Grimes, Collin Sexton, Kevon Looney, Matisse Thybulle and Cameron Carr.

So far, so good. The Lakers are 11-2 on the season and have jelled nicely, even if there are some questions about whether the team can hold up in the playoffs against some of the elite teams in the sport.

Regardless, the Lakers built their team completely around Dončić's skill set, and any injury to him is a massive concern. If the Lakers are going to win their first title since the Orlando bubble, they'll need Dončić healthy and thriving.

articles.title: 'Panic Decision,' Mikal Bridges Benching Addressed by Mike Brown After Knicks' Loss to Harden, Cavs
articles.summary: Mikal Bridges has had a rough start to the 2026-27 campaign, and it's fair to wonder whether New York Knicks head coach Mike Brown is considering bringing him off the bench rather than starting him.
articles.body:
Mikal Bridges has had a rough start to the 2026-27 campaign, and it's fair to wonder whether New York Knicks head coach Mike Brown is considering bringing him off the bench rather than starting him.

After Bridges was benched in the fourth quarter of Wednesday's game against the Cleveland Cavaliers, Brown said he doesn't plan on making a "panic decision."

"Mikal has a proven track record of playing at a pretty high level as a starter in this league," Brown said . "For me to make a 'panic decision' and change it right now, 10 games in or whatever we are, I'm not feeling it."

Brown did recognize, however, that Landry Shamet and Deuce McBride's high level of play this year has made it difficult to balance out the minutes.

"Part of it is you have two guys that are playing really well in Landy and Deuce, so it's gonna be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal, and maybe at times for Josh (Hart)," Brown said. "Because those two guys are playing at a pretty high level. Not just on the offensive side of the floor but defensively too."

Bridges is putting up 6.3 points, 3.4 rebounds and 2.1 assists per game while shooting just 32.9 percent from the field and 26.5 percent from deep, on pace for career lows in a number of categories.

He's averaged 25.1 minutes per game so far, but just 20.8 over the Knicks' last five games.

Bridges is clearly working through some struggles, but it appears Brown plans to keep him in the starting lineup for now. If things don't start clicking soon, though, Brown might have no choice but to make a change.

Houston's Marcus Smart got into it with Golden State's Charles Bassey after a hard foul, and Smart eventually threw a punch at Bassey, earning him a flagrant 2 and an automatic ejection.

The fight was broken up relatively swiftly, but not fast enough to avoid a punch. The ejection marked the 13th of Smart's career.

articles.title: Rockets G Marcus Smart ejected after throwing punch at Warriors' Charles Bassey
articles.summary: Smart can likely expect a suspension coming his way from the NBA.
articles.body:
Marcus Smart missed the fourth quarter of the Houston Rockets' game against the Golden State Warriors. The NBA might decide he needs to miss even more time.

The veteran guard was ejected on a Flagrant 2 foul after throwing a punch at Warriors center Charles Bassey in the final minutes of the third quarter. The dispute appeared to be instigated when the two players got tangled up on a rebound, with Smart throwing the punch moments later.

Smart clearly knew what was coming after the punch, as he immediately walked off the court rather than wait to hear the officials' ruling. Judging from the replay, it's unclear if the punch even made contact.

Per Matt Young of the Houston Chronicle , Rockets head coach Ime Udoka said after the game that Smart confronted Bassey about wrapping up his elbow on the rebound, to which Bassey replied, "What you gonna do?" Smart responded with the punch.

After the game, Bassey called Smart's punch "fake toughness."

"He's been playing dirty the whole game," Bassey said, according to Yahoo Sports' Kelly Iko . "I don't think he was trying to play, I think he was trying to get kicked out of the game."

Not only was Smart ejected, he can also expect a mandatory fine for the flagrant foul as well as a likely suspension from the NBA. The league's rulebook is fairly clear on that matter :

Any player who throws a punch, whether it connects or not, has committed an unsportsmanlike act. He will be ejected following confirmation during review by instant replay and suspended for a minimum of one game.

Smart exited the game with 6 points on 2-for-2 shooting (both 3-pointers), 2 rebounds, 1 assist, 1 turnover and 4 personal fouls in 17 minutes. His early exit didn't prevent the Rockets from winning 115-108 , in a game that also saw the Warriors lose Stephen Curry to an injury in the first quarter .

The Golden State Warriors were unable to overcome the early departure of Stephen Curry on Wednesday night, falling to the Houston Rockets by the final score of 115-108 at the Toyota Center.

Curry only played six minutes in the first quarter before he was ruled out for the remainder of the game due to right abdominal soreness .

Here's a look at how stars from both teams including Kevin Durant and Draymond Green fared during the contest:

The Rockets got off to a hot start, opening the game on a 17-7 run before leading 35-20 at the end of the first quarter.

Golden State cut into the deficit by outscoring Houston 28-21 in the second quarter, but the Rockets still held an eight-point advantage at halftime.

Houston took another double-digit lead near the beginning of the third quarter and maintained it for the majority of the period, although the game was briefly stopped after Rockets guard Marcus Smart threw a punch at Warriors center Charles Bassey.

The Warriors pulled within eight points early in the fourth quarter before Houston immediately responded with a 15-2 run, putting the game out of reach for Golden State.

The Rockets now sit at 9-3, while the Warriors dropped to 8-4.

articles.title: Why was Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart ejected? All about clash with Golden State Warriors center Charles Bassey
articles.summary: Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart was ejected from Wednesday night’s game against the Golden State Warriors after throwing a punch at Warriors center
articles.body: Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart was ejected from Wednesday night’s game against the Golden State Warriors after throwing a punch at Warriors center Charles Bassey. It happened with 21 seconds left in the third quarter, right after Amen Thompson scored on a three-point play in transition. Houston was ahead at the time. Smart and Bassey went face-to-face at the top of the key, and his right hand seemed to fall just short of Bassey’s face. The two were pulled apart. Smart stormed off to the locker room, and officials eventually ruled him out.Why was Marcus Smart ejected from the Warriors game?Officials went to the NBA Replay Center in Secaucus, New Jersey, to look at the clash between Marcus Smart and Charles Bassey. They came back with a Flagrant 2 on Smart. The call covers contact judged unnecessary and excessive. A Flagrant 1 would have brought the same two free throws and possession for the offended team, but Smart would have stayed in the game. The Flagrant 2 added the ejection. So Golden State got two free throws and the ball, while Houston lost its guard on the same play.Smart did not wait for the verdict. He was already off the floor while officials sorted it out, and ESPN analyst Doris Burke had no doubt how it would end. “You didn’t even need to tell him, he knew he was gone,” Burke said during the broadcast. She added, “That’s absolutely a punch.”Bassey stayed in the game, so the penalty landed on the Rockets guard alone. The play also put Bassey in an odd spot. He was part of the exchange yet stayed in the game, and Golden State kept its center on the floor for the rest of the night. One call was enough. Another technical or flagrant foul was never needed.Smart Finishes with six points in 16 minutes for HoustonSmart’s night ended with six points and two rebounds in 16 minutes. Houston entered the fourth with a lead to hold and one fewer guard to hold it. Teammates had to cover the minutes Smart would have played. The exchange also pulled attention away from the basketball Houston needed to play with a lead on the line.A Flagrant 2 settles the penalty inside the game and does not automatically bring a suspension. articles.body: Los Oklahoma City Thunder, con Aday Mara (21 años y 2,21 m.) como titular, perdieron 118-108 ante los Portand Trail Blazers en la NBA. Deni Avdija (28 puntos), Damian Lillard (18 puntos), Jrue Holiday (19 puntos) y Donovan Clingan (5 puntos y 12 rebotes) lideraron a Portland para cerrar una serie de dos victorias contra Oklahoma. articles.title: Ibon Navarro: "El Real Madrid te mete 100 puntos sin querer"
articles.standfirst: El entrenador del Estrella Roja, segundo clasificado de la Euroliga, analiza el duelo de esta noche (21.00 horas) ante el equipo blanco y cuenta cómo es su vida en Belgrado
articles.summary: El entrenador del Estrella Roja, segundo clasificado de la Euroliga, analiza el duelo de esta noche (21.00 horas) ante el equipo blanco y cuenta cómo es su vida en Belgrado
articles.body: La aventura de Ibon Navarro (Vitoria, 1976) en el Estrella Roja difícilmente podía haber arrancado mejor. Con un equipo muy renovado, marcha segundo en la Euroliga justo antes de visitar este jueves (21.00 horas) al Real Madrid. Sobre los dos conjuntos, su vida en Belgrado, la pasión por el baloncesto allí y el auge de los técnicos españoles habla en esta charla. Pregunta. ¿Cómo van las cosas por Belgrado? Respuesta. Ya sabes: cuando ganas, están mejor. La primera semana estaba todo el mundo tenso y luego la gente se ha ido calmando y está feliz. Aquí se vive todo muy intensamente. El fútbol en España, aquí es el baloncesto. P. Según está la clasificación, gana uno dos partidos seguidos y es segundo, pero si los pierde es octavo... R. Claro. Nosotros ahora tenemos seguidos fuera Real Madrid, Milán y Barcelona. El calendario cuenta mucho. Llevamos sólo 10 jornadas. P. Sí, pero segundos de la Euroliga suena muy bien. R. Empatados con el séptimo, eh. Al final es muy circunstancial. Que sí, que se está mejor siendo segundo que duodécimo, pero es circunstancial. No le damos mucha importancia. P. ¿No se ven dando guerra durante mucho tiempo? La verdad es que hay unos transatlánticos en la Euroliga... R. Es que es muy pronto. Nosotros hemos jugado seis partidos en casa y cuatro fuera. De los cuatro, el que hemos perdido fue en Belgrado, el derbi. Pero en casa hemos perdido los dos primeros y contra equipos que son de pelear con nosotros, como Hapoel y Zalgiris. Esto es una locura de competición. Ahora puedes ganar casi a cualquiera y perder casi con cualquiera. Ya más adelante, cuando empieza a haber dinámicas es distinto. Ahora todos los partidos son muy difíciles. P. En el buen inicio influyen lo bien que han encajado todas las piezas aunque había muchos jugadores nuevos. En Málaga ya hizo funcionar muy pronto a un equipo con muchos fichajes. ¿Cómo lo consigue? R. La columna vertebral, al menos a nivel deportivo, sí que se ha mantenido: Butler, Nwora, Ojeleye, Moneke, el núcleo de los serbios... Ellos ya tienen cierto conocimiento. Luego, incorporar jugadores que sabes que funcionan y que entienden esto: Chris Jones, que ha estado en España y sabes lo que da; Weiler-Babb, que está muy europeizado por los años que lleva aquí; David Kramer, que ha estado en la ACB... Son buenos jugadores y sabes que son buenas personas. No solamente es una cuestión de sumar talento, sino de encontrar también jugadores que aporten cierto conocimiento de algunas cosas y hagan equipo. A partir de ahí, buscar cierta química, que la gente esté más o menos cohesionada, que tengan todos objetivos comunes y que los antepongan a los personales. Ahora en noviembre se puede hacer, pero ya más adelante, a partir de abril-mayo, es más difícil cuando los jugadores empiezan a escuchar cantos de sirena, que si te voy a fichar aquí, que si te voy a fichar allá, que si hay ya ofertas millonarias. Ahora todavía sí que puedes meter a la gente en los objetivos de equipo. P. Son el mejor equipo defensivo de la Euroliga: reciben sólo 74 puntos, tiene el mejor rating defensivo, vienen de dejar al Olympiacos en 57... ¿La defensa es el principio de todo? R. Nos hemos enfocado mucho en mejorar algunos aspectos defensivos, porque el equipo tiene mucho talento. Eso nos ha llevado a tener muy poca frescura en las primeras semanas, con porcentajes muy bajos a pesar de que el equipo se pasaba bastante bien el balón y le daba muchos tiros, aunque nos costaba llegar a 80 puntos. Pero era capaz de competir a través del trabajo defensivo. No nos dio para ganar los primeros dos días, pero a partir de ahí fuimos a Dubái y creo que recibimos 58. Yo creo que el equipo, en líneas generales, estaba bien trabajado el año pasado, porque tanto Sfairopoulos como Sasa Obradovic son entrenadores que trabajan mucho aspectos defensivos, pero tenía algunas carencias, sobre todo a nivel de balance. Era un equipo al que mentalmente le costaba mucho gestionar la frustración de los errores y nos hemos centrado mucho en eso, en intentar que no tenga parones en las fases de juego, de ataque a defensa, defensa a ataque, porque ahí es donde sufría mucho. Era el equipo de la Euroliga que más puntos recibía en campo abierto. En medio campo era la quinta mejor defensa y las cuatro primeras estuvieron en la Final Four. Por eso nos hemos centrado mucho en el balance defensivo. Creo que los chicos están haciendo un muy buen trabajo y el equipo ha ido mejorando. P. Ahora visitan al Real Madrid, que tiene uno de los mejores ataques de la Euroliga y le encanta correr. R. Te mete 100 puntos sin querer. Es un poco el sello de Pedro [Martínez], de mantener ese ritmo muy alto. Es verdad que les puede pesar un poco la falta del Facu [Campazzo], pero sin él y sin algunos jugadores en otras posiciones, llevaron al Panathinaikos a la prórroga. Juegan con mucho ritmo, muchas posesiones y con jugadores muy buenos en tomar decisiones en campo abierto, lo que les hace súper peligrosos. P. ¿Le sorprendió, como a muchos, el fichaje de Pedro Martínez por el Real Madrid? R. Eso no era raro. Lo raro era que Pedro nunca hubiera entrenado en alguno de los grandes. Para muchos de nosotros que lo hemos tenido enfrente en Gran Canaria, Manresa, Valencia... era un referente en muchas cosas y nunca lo habíamos visto ni en un Barça ni en un Madrid. Sí que había estado en el Baskonia o el Valencia, que también son equipos muy punteros, pero faltaba ese aura que te dan el Barça y el Madrid. Lo extraño era que no hubiera pasado antes. Los grandes clubes tienen que tener grandes entrenadores y tanto el Madrid como Pedro lo son. P. Ustedes, los entrenadores unos años más jóvenes, ¿le ven como un referente? R. Por la parte que me toca, lo que más me ha gustado siempre de él y lo que más he admirado es su capacidad de reinventarse, de ir añadiendo cosas nuevas y de copiar cosas, pero luego hacerlas suyas y darle su toque. Hay entrenadores que han sido súper exitosos y siguen haciendo lo mismo porque han ganado muchas cosas de esa manera, pero Pedro tiene ese inconformismo de no quedarse en una zona de confort. Evoluciona e intenta hacer algo nuevo. Estábamos todos mirando qué iba a hacer en el Madrid después de haber visto lo que había hecho en Valencia y nos preguntábamos qué iba a hacer con un jugador como Tavares, por ejemplo. Pues está consiguiendo que Tavares haga cosas que nunca había hecho. Esa es la grandeza que tiene Pedro: hay que adaptarse a él, pero también consigue que jugadores de ese nivel compren su filosofía. Tienes que tener caché y carisma para conseguirlo. P. Que haya siete entrenadores españoles en Euroliga, incluidos los dos de Belgrado, era algo inimaginable hace poco. ¿Se puede hablar de una escuela española igual que hubo una exitosa escuela yugoslava de entrenadores? R. No sé si es circunstancial. Sí que se valoran ciertas cosas del entrenador español a nivel de conocimientos, de gestión... Pero cuando te pones a hablar de esto parece que estás diciendo que otros no hacen cosas bien. El mayor éxito del entrenador español es que no tenemos ningún problema en salir de España para trabajar. Antes costaba un poco más. Recuerdo que Joan Plaza fue el primero que dio ese paso de salir a un equipo de Euroliga cuando se fue al Zalgiris. Y eso al margen de los que hay en Centroamérica y Sudamérica. Salir de esa zona de confort es lo que mejor habla de nosotros. P. En Serbia se tiene un respeto reverencial a los entrenadores. ¿Lo ha notado? R. Sí, es cierto. Se tiene mucho respeto a la figura del entrenador, más allá de rivalidades. Todo el mundo es muy consciente de que tú eres el que gestiona muchas cosas, todo tiene que pasar por ti y tienes que estar al tanto de todo. Eres una figura muy respetada. Esa es la palabra. Y no sólo por la gente del Estrella Roja. Tanto a Joan [Peñarroya, entrenador del Partizan] la gente del Estrella Roja como a mí la del Partizan, notamos que te dicen: "Oye, yo soy del rival, pero...". Siempre te tratan con mucho respeto. P. ¿Le reconocen por la calle? ¿Le paran? R. Sí, sí. Vivimos en una zona donde hay mucho extranjero y a veces pasas un poco desapercibido, pero en cuanto no es así, sí que te conoce todo el mundo. P. Cuando hablé recientemente con Joan Peñarroya me dijo que tenían muy buena relación pero que no se pueden tomar ni un café juntos porque, dada la rivalidad con el Partizan, se forma un buen lío. R. Es así. En público, imposible. Y eso que vivimos cerca el uno del otro. P. Más allá del resultado, que perdieron, ¿cómo fue su primera experiencia en un derbi de Belgrado? ¿Impresiona tanto y encima como visitante? R. Me impresionó mucho el ambiente previo. No quisiera decir la palabra odio, pero sí que se parece mucho a la relación que hay entre los dos equipos. Luego, una vez que empiezas el partido, realmente estás al juego y no eres muy consciente de lo que hay. Recuerdo que los aficionados del Estrella Roja entraron más tarde al pabellón y sí que se armó una buena, con bengalas que iban de un lado a otro, algún cohete que hizo que se parara el partido. Carlos Peruga era uno de los árbitros y alguna vez se nos quedaba mirando a Joan y a mí y levantábamos las cejas como: "¿Esto qué es?". Fue muy intenso, la verdad. No voy a tener un gran recuerdo porque perdimos en la prórroga, pero sí que fue una experiencia inolvidable. P. Firmó por dos años. ¿Le va a dar tiempo a aprender serbio? R. Bueno, estoy en ello, aunque me han recomendado que no lo haga. Todo el mundo cree que es mejor que no entienda ni periódicos, ni podcast, ni redes sociales, ni televisión, ni nada. Pero ya no es una cuestión solamente de adaptarte, sino de aprender cosas. Estuve en Manresa y Andorra y también lo intenté.

articles.title: 1 Overreaction To Every NBA Team's Start
articles.summary: It typically takes about a quarter of a season for NBA teams to start forming an identity and separating sustainable fact from small-sample fiction.
articles.body:
It typically takes about a quarter of a season for NBA teams to start forming an identity and separating sustainable fact from small-sample fiction.

Fortunately for the rest of us, it doesn't take nearly as long to throw together some early-season overreactions.

With 10-ish games played for just about every side, now is the perfect time to lay out an overreaction for all 30 teams, examining both why they've emerged and how they could prove to be nothing more than premature verdicts.

ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

Overreaction: Jalen Johnson can't lead this franchise.

Hoop heads are always plugged into the follow-up efforts of a previous season's breakout star, and this season has been no different. So when Johnson, a first-time All-Star and All-NBA honoree in 2025-26, opened this campaign in less than electric fashion, folks became less convinced about his ability to guide this group where it wants to go.

That already feels laughable given all the different ways he can loudly impact the game. Already this season—when his shooting rates are down, mind you—he has authored the following stat lines: 30 points, seven rebounds, six assists; 26 points, 16 assists and nine rebounds; 21 points, nine rebounds and two blocks; and 20 points, 14 rebounds and six assists.

Oh, and he's done all of the above while navigating around an ankle sprain. His arrow is still pointing all the way up. His shots will fall at a higher clip, and Atlanta will better position him for success by upping its on-ball options around him ( more Kingston Flemings floor time, please ).

Overreaction: They're better without Jaylen Brown.

The Celtics proved last season they can be plenty feisty when following the lead of a solo star. And, honestly, given the kind of heater Paul George has been on to start this campaign, you could argue Boston has a co-star for Jayson Tatum again.

But recent history suggests George might be playing over his head. Or maybe his run gets upended by availability issues again.

Either way, there's a real chance the Shamrocks are a solo-star squad now, which is a formula the league almost never regards as championship-caliber. And this certainly won't be the exception if Jayson Tatum fails to significantly elevate his sagging shooting rates (42.5 percent overall, 32.4 percent from range).

Overreaction: The kids are not all right.

Shouldn't a team that made seven first-round picks over the last two drafts be seeing a lot more encouraging signs from its young core than Brooklyn has so far? Ideally, sure, but the take lacks nuance.

Mikel Brown Jr. has received the kid-glove treatment as a cautious response to the back trouble that limited him at Louisville. Egor Dëmin made just four appearances before being shelved by a bone bruise in his right leg. Rookie first-rounder Joshua Jefferson battled preseason back soreness and landed in the G League shortly thereafter.

Conditions have been less than ideal, and that's without factoring in the Nets' need to showcase trade candidates Michael Porter Jr. and Julius Randle. And still, Brooklyn has found encouragement from Nolan Traoré and Danny Wolf. Hope may not extend to the entire young core, but it reaches more than it doesn't.

Overreaction: They're lost without LaMelo.

When Charlotte split from franchise face, longtime floor general and identity-setter LaMelo Ball this summer, it took a massive step into the unknown.

The footing-finding process never figured to be fast, and it has only proved harder to handle with the injury bug bothering both Kon Knueppel and Coby White. Things have looked rough so far (4-7 with a bottom-five net rating ), but that probably should have been the expectation, particularly in light of these injury issues.

Things are rarely as bad (or as good) as they seem in this league, and this situation feels no different. Give the Hornets healthy versions of Knueppel and White, a better integrated Naz Reid and up-to-speed editions of Hannes Steinbach and Christian Anderson Jr., and they should find their new way sooner than later.

Overreaction: They should have never signed Norman Powell.

Chicago's two-year, $45 million pact with Powell ranked high among this summer's top surprises. And Bulls fans have already started to see why with Powell looking both out of place as a 33-year-old on this rebuilding roster and underqualified to fill such a prominent role in an offense with so many players who are finding their way.

The results haven't been pretty; Chicago is 26th in offensive rating, and Powell has his worst true shooting percentage in nearly a decade ( 57.7 ). But this was never about seeing immediate results, and things won't always look this rough.

Powell is a much better shooter than he has shown, and that will be easier to showcase as his young teammates get more comfortable contributing to the offense. And once Powell puts together a solid stretch, he'll probably be shipped out to a win-now shopper for long-term assets—as has likely been the plan all along.

Nothing about the start of Harden's age-37 season has been the slightest bit encouraging.

He had been losing scoring volume and efficiency in recent years, but those hits have never come harder (15.3 points, career-low 54.1 percent true shooting). He previously compensated with copious amounts of playmaking, but that's drying up too (5.7 assists, his fewest ever as a full-time starter).

It's an outright panic in Northeast Ohio, and maybe this is the brutal beginning of a fast-forwarded free-fall. Or perhaps this historically prolific producer (a three-time scoring champ and former MVP) is just uncharacteristically off with his shot and adapting on the fly to what's still a pretty new offensive environment for him.

Harden may not bounce back, but it's way too early to say with certainty that he can't.

Overreaction: The Kyrie Irving trade chatter needs to stop.

Remember Dallas' constant denial of Irving's availability this summer? Maybe the Mavericks were onto something. Because when Irving shares the floor with franchise face Cooper Flagg, this team looks like a juggernaut ( plus-13.6 net rating across 190 minutes).

"We're excited because they're both such versatile players," first-year Mavericks coach Dusty May told reporters . "They shoot it, they drive it, they share it. It's going to be a fun puzzle."

The pieces have proved a fun (and wildly effective) fit so far, but that still doesn't mean they come from the same puzzle. Flagg is still a teenager, and Irving will turn 35 in March. Whatever window they have, it won't stay open for long. That's why the trade speculation will not (and should not) stop soon.

Overreaction: Nikola Jokić is on the decline.

The unguardable version of Jokić who has controlled the best-player-on-the-planet debates and largely factored into the MVP races for the last decade has been absent.

He has still been really good, obviously, but this isn't his typical greatness: fewest points per game since 2019-20 (23.1), second-fewest assists in his last five seasons (9.1), worst field-goal and three-point percentages of his career (48.8 and 22.5, respectively). Is Denver seeing the start of his decline?

That's probably within the realm of possibilities, but it's on the extreme end of unlikelihoods. Folks wouldn't even notice a shaky nine-game shooting stretch if it happened later in the season, and maybe he's still feeling the effects of the knee trouble that sidelined him for a month around the new year. It's way too early to start penning any obituaries.

Detroit has a .700 winning percentage and the NBA's seventh-best rating . It has a viable three-point attack now (12th in makes, ninth in percentage). It's holding top-10 rankings in assists (seventh) and turnovers (eighth).

Clearly, all is well in the Motor City, right? Not so fast, my friend.

The Pistons seem even more pressed for non-Cade Cunningham scoring and shot-creation than they were last season. Shooting specialist Duncan Robinson is their No. 2 scorer right now—and only player other than Cade averaging more than 13 points per outing. Detroit needs to find a legitimate co-star and fast.

Remember when the Warriors were left for dead on the heels of a largely listless 0-3 start? Well, they embarked on a sizzling eight-game winning streak and paced everyone in net rating over that stretch ( plus-16.4 ). Yaxel Lendeborg is the early Rookie of the Year favorite, and Stephen Curry, at 38 years young, has been presenting a credible MVP case.

Did the Dubs just author one of the most impressive switch-flips in recent history? Sure. Are they just full-fledged heavyweight contenders again? Probably not.

Some parts of this surge feel sustainable, but all of them? That seems a stretch.

The most alarming element came when Curry left Wednesday's streak-stopping loss to the Rockets because of abdominal soreness.

Beyond that, the Warriors could still be pesky playoff opponents, but to become more they'll need Curry and Jimmy Butler—and, to a lesser extent, Moses Moody—back sooner than later with no signs of rust, and they have to find a way to turn Kristaps Porziņģis and draft capital into something interesting on the trade market.

Overreaction: Jabari Smith Jr. is making the leap.

There are myriad reasons why the Rockets have seemingly launched into the top-shelf contender tier. The best-to-date breakout from Smith is a quietly big part of this success.

The 6'11" swingman has turned his stat sheet into a string of personal bests. He has never averaged more points (17), more assists (2.4), more stocks (1.8) or fewer turnovers (0.9). He has also never posted better shooting rates from the field (50.4%), from three (44.8%) or at the line (86.2%).

Maybe the stars are all aligning, but it's more likely there's some fun with numbers tied to a couple of huge outings. He's had 30 points twice and 22 points another time; otherwise, it's been his typical mid-teens output with good-not-great shooting lines.

When the Pacers last had a healthy Tyrese Haliburton, they finished one win shy of a championship. While they don't technically have his healthy version now—he has missed two weeks with a hamstring strain—they weren't exactly in championship form before he went down.

They've been bullied on the boards. They can't find their collective shooting touch from the perimeter or at the stripe. Their defense isn't making enough plays to compensate for an offense lagging behind its typical output.

But doesn't this seem like it might be a cold spell? They're a better shooting team than this. And their rebounding issue might be alleviated by more normal doses of Ivica Zubac (who's already been both banged-up and minutes-restricted). Give them time to get healthy and gel, and they could be an Eastern Conference factor yet.

L.A.'s long-term outlook took a major hit when the NBA stripped the Clippers of five first-round picks after finding violations of its salary-cap circumvention rules. And rookie Keaton Wagler's early shooting struggles—32.9 percent from the field—haven't offered much encouragement.

All hope doesn't have to be lost, though. Not yet, anyway.

Wagler has almost limitless time to grow. The youth movement will get a little rosier whenever Yanic Konan Niederhäuser (foot) returns to action. And this club has a chance to restock some draft capital with at least a handful of plug-and-play veterans to shop around between now and the deadline.

Overreaction: They have joined the circle of trust.

Holy smokes, what a start in Hollywood. The Lakers refashioned their roster around Luka Dončić this summer, and he has rewarded that trust by basically rebooting Wilt Chamberlain's old output ( 1.08 points per minute! ).

Dončić is defending now, too . Austin Reaves is averaging 25 points and applying for 50/40/90 club membership. Walker Kessler is rim-running his way to near 70-percent shooting. Collectively, the Lakers' offense is dusting the field ( 121.5 points per 100 possessions, 2.5 more than the No. 2 attack).

This is a scorching-hot start, but it can't be labeled as anything more yet. There are still questions about this defense, which sits a forgettable 19th in efficiency , and the on-paper improvements to this group's depth haven't made it to the court.

The previous possessor of a largely anonymous NBA existence, Jerome is suddenly producing like a true offensive elite. He is one of only seven players averaging at least 25 points, 4.5 assists and 2.5 three-pointers, and his 63.1 percent true shooting is third-highest among that exclusive group.

Three players have earned Western Conference Player of the Week honors so far this season: Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama and Jerome. Just like we all envisioned, right?

Jerome has shattered all realistic (and uber-optimistic) expectations and almost assuredly leveled up. His downhill drives are slippery, his floater is pure and his three-ball is fiery. But let's do some brake-pumping on All-Star buzz. He'll need a whole lot more than a couple of strong weeks to build that case.

Overreaction: Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo can't fit.

The Heat hoped for years to have a shot at rostering Antetokounmpo. And now that he's finally strolling the sands of South Beach, they don't have a roster capable of supporting him. That's the early-season read of the situation at least.

"I never thought [Antetokounmpo and Adebayo] were going to fit together," one executive told The Ringer's Howard Beck . "I just don't know how you run an offense with two power forwards. Neither one of them can shoot and operate in the same space."

The results have been brutal so far— minus-5.1 net rating over the pair's 209 shared minutes—but that might have more to do with the perimeter problems around the bigs than the twin towers themselves.

Give mastermind coach Erik Spoelstra more time to figure this out and the front office more chances to shore up weak spots before abandoning hope on Miami's talented twosome.

Overreaction: Ryan Rollins was a one-year wonder.

Rollins entered last season with three NBA go-rounds on his resume and a 5.1 career scoring average. He exited it with per-game averages of 17.3 points, 5.6 assists and 1.5 steals and a fifth-placed finish in Most Improved Player voting.

Since this new campaign tipped, though, he's gone back to being a pumpkin. His output collapsed and took his floor time with it. He's down to just 11 points and 4.1 assists, though his steals have risen to 1.7. All three percentages in his 39.8/37.3/66.7 shooting split have also declined.

It's an uncomfortable development—particularly for anyone hoping he'd reach building block status for the post-Giannis Bucks—but it may be nothing more than a small-sample mirage.

Everyone in Milwaukee is getting comfortable with one another (and most might be auditioning for other teams), so once that settles, maybe Rollins can just pick up where he left off.

Overreaction: LaMelo Ball has changed the narrative.

This summer, the Wolves effectively wagered their championship hopes on Ball being their missing piece—and maybe nailed the bet?

Their offense is humming, they are navigating Anthony Edwards' injury absence just fine, and they're making Ball look like a vital piece of their winning formula.

So much for that unserious reputation , right? Maybe, but let's see how things look come playoff time.

Because, remember, Ball's next playoff minutes will be his first. And if he goes cold or gets too loose with the basketball at the wrong time, the criticism could return and the takes could burn hotter than ever. It's been a fun start, but that's all it's been.

Overreaction: They should have liquidated their veterans already.

The Pelicans have protected this roster like it's one of the very best in the league. Or at least, like it could become that if the players ever stayed healthy.

Well, they've had most everyone available this season and just don't look like a good team. The offense is average, the defense is bad and the total package is blah (4-7 with a bottom-third net rating ).

Should this core have been swapped out for draft assets by now? Probably, yeah, but there shouldn't be much (if any) damage from waiting. The vets aren't losing their trade value—Trey Murphy III might be the most coveted trade target in the league—and their young players aren't hurting for developmental touches and floor time.

Overreaction: They can't defend their throne.

How long does a championship hangover last again? Don't blame New York for not knowing, since its summer title run snapped a championship drought that spanned more than five decades.

The Knicks have trotted through a sluggish 6-4 start. The same starting five that consistently crushed postseason competition is now losing its minutes by 8.1 points per 100 possessions.

This isn't ideal, obviously, but it's also not a reason to panic. They've dealt with unnecessary distractions , felt the effects of such a grueling postseason and generally drawn everyone's best shot. They've also missed a lot of makeable shots, and as those start finding their mark, the club should get back to its winning ways.

Overreaction: Injuries knocked them out of the circle of trust.

The injury bug has been a problematically present character in the early stages of this season, and perhaps no one has felt its wrath more than OKC.

In a matter of days, the Thunder lost Jalen Williams (dislocated ankle, fractured fibula), Cason Wallace (torn labrum) and Chet Holmgren (patellar tendon tear), or 60 percent of their starting lineup.

Holmgren could miss multiple months. Williams and Wallace might be lost for the entire campaign. Even a team as deep as this one can't withstand knockout blows like that, right?

Well, the Thunder are doing everything they can to prove their resiliency and championship grit. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is playing at an MVP level, Ajay Mitchell is aiming to fill the co-star role, the defense looks stingy as always and rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz are both hitting the ground running. OKC clearly isn't going down without a serious fight.

After three consecutive first-round exits, the Magic axed former coach Jamahl Mosley and affixed their hopes to Sean Sweeney. They somehow look even farther from contention now with a .300 winning percentage and an awful minus-7.1 net rating (24th).

Is it time for Orlando to give up on this specific group and start changing out some puzzle pieces? Not yet.

Maybe the Magic make that concession later this season, but these early struggles feel tied to injury trouble more than anything. They need a long look at how Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner fit with Sweeney at the helm before deciding they don't want to move forward with such a potentially potent pair of skilled big forwards.

Overreaction: The kitchen is overcrowded with cooks.

The Sixers have two former MVPs (LeBron James, Joel Embiid), two All-NBA honorees from last season (Jaylen Brown, Tyrese Maxey) and a first-team selection from the 2025-26 All-Rookie teams (VJ Edgecombe). They also have the 22nd-ranked offense by efficiency. Huh?

"Every five starters that we have are playing a different role than they played last year, and some of them probably ever," Maxey told reporters . "… I think we're all trying to adapt and figure it out. I mean, it's going to take time."

That's the thing: Even superteams can't control time. This roster has so many moving pieces, and all of them are still aligning. Also, it's still November. The season has a long way to go, meaning there is tons of time to figure out how to turn this offense into a multiplaymaker, score-from-anywhere machine.

Overreaction: They won't make the Play-In.

The Suns sometimes make it way too easy for their fans to feel like the sky is falling. Like, say, when they interpret the need for a Devin Booker co-star as rationale for sacrificing a future first-round pick for Miles Bridges. Or sabotage their own offense (and increase their own frustration ) by neglecting the point guard position.

Trusting this team isn't easy, because sometimes it just no-shows. Like when it starts a new season on the wrong end of a 21-0 run.

Writing it off this early into the campaign still feels foolish. The West has more winnable games and fewer juggernauts than normal. The Suns won't be a major factor in the conference race, but saying they can't lock down a top-10 seed is selling them short.

Overreaction: They can and should keep all of their guards.

The Blazers have four point guards on the roster, and they all qualify as prominent players.

Damian Lillard and Ja Morant have been true franchise faces. Jrue Holiday has been an All-Star and a key contributor on two title teams. Scoot Henderson, while less celebrated than the rest, entered the league with enormous expectations as the third overall pick in 2023.

It doesn't feel like this should work, but it is working . Portland has seven wins in 10 tries and a top-five offense leading the way.

This still doesn't feel like the best way to maximize a roster. Especially when the wings could use reinforcing behind starters Deni Avdija and Toumani Camara. And especially especially when this isn't working for Henderson and is muting Holiday's impact.

Overreaction: They're having Darius Acuff Jr. build bad habits.

The Kings have a veteran core they'd like to unload, and a youth movement that is grossly underpopulated. There isn't much going on in Sacramento other than Acuff, so the club is letting him explore the full limits of his game (22.8 shots, 32.2 usage percentage ) and perhaps exposing him to more losing than he can handle.

This level of losing will test his competitive resolve. And he might be handling more responsibilities now than he will during his peak.

That doesn't mean this is all a bad thing. The experimentation will allow him to test the full limits of his game. The challenge of shouldering such a heavy burden could result in his refusal to accept anything but his best. And all of this losing should be (at least in theory) temporary pain.

The Spurs look unstoppable. Or they do when the starters are on the floor, at least. With Victor Wembanyama perhaps cracking the basketball code, and San Antonio's three-headed monster at guard keeping defenses perpetually uncomfortable, the Spurs' first five looks like the ultimate cheat code.

Get to the bench, though, and San Antonio looks, uh, stoppable. The second-teamers sit 19th in offensive efficiency and 18th in net rating. The hope for this unit has backtracked from creating advantages to merely treading water.

But it has the personnel needed to do so much more. Tobias Harris (calf) still hasn't debuted, and he could be a game-changer. Keldon Johnson probably didn't just forget how to shoot over the offseason. Harrison Barnes is capable of more. And if Luke Kornet can't find his footing, San Antonio could turn things over to rookie first-rounder Tarris Reed Jr.

Overreaction: They can't count on Kawhi Leonard.

Nothing inspired more north-of-the-border hope this offseason than Leonard's return to the Raptors. But his latest bout with knee trouble has limited him to the point of near-disappearance: two appearances totaling 52 minutes across the club's first 10 contests.

And, while this may be nothing given the miniature sample size, he didn't exactly wow folks with his play before going down. In those games, he had 39 points on 37 shots and more turnovers (four) than assists (three).

Toronto fans shouldn't be worried. Not in the middle of November. His body requires maintenance, and he might just be getting patched up earlier than normal.

Nothing from Leonard's injury updates has raised red flags, and everything from his 2025-26 All-NBA effort should have Toronto fans giddy about what he'll do when he's ready to return.

The Jazz spent at least parts of the past few seasons trying to lose. They are ostensibly not trying to lose any longer, though you wouldn't know it from all of the losing they've been doing (1-10 with a minus-11.1 net rating).

This is not intentional. It's also not surprising since the normal starting frontcourt—Lauri Markkanen, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Jusuf Nurkić—is all stuck on the sidelines. Leading scorer Keyonte George missed the last outing, too.

The Jazz are going through it: dealing with injuries, navigating growing pains and hoping a roster used to losing on purpose can learn how to win on the fly. They'll turn things around, if not in time to challenge for this season's play-in, then at least to generate excitement about the full-strength possibilities for next season.

Overreaction: They're stunting Alex Sarr's growth.

The Wizards are having slightly better luck with their attempted acceleration, but this still feels like a mishmash of mostly young players who don't know how to win and veterans who need to win right now. Some players are making it work, but the transition has been tough for Sarr.

His minutes have mostly held steady, but his offensive involvement is way down. Over his first two seasons, he averaged 12.9 shots and had a 24.4 usage percentage. Now, he's down to just 8.0 shots and has a 16.8 percent usage rate.

The double-big look with Sarr and Anthony Davis isn't working, but it should be temporary. And Sarr should be better off rethinking how he can make more out of less, since he is unlikely to fill more than a supporting role on a competitive team.

articles.title: Top 25 Men's College Basketball Transfers Making an Immediate Impact
articles.summary: It has become almost impossible to build a competent men's college basketball roster without at least dipping a toe into the transfer portal.
articles.body:
It has become almost impossible to build a competent men's college basketball roster without at least dipping a toe into the transfer portal.

By my count ( per Verbal Commits ), there were 1,708 transfers from one D-I school to another this past offseason. Power Five programs added 449 players via the portal, and 201 of those came from other P5 schools.

Needless to say, there are a lot of star faces in new places. Many of them are already making a major impact in their new homes.

To a considerable extent, preseason expectations (both for player and team) matter. But rest assured, breakout stars like Memphis' Jayden Reid, Iowa State's Tre Singleton and UCF's Dior Johnson feature prominently on this list, even though they wouldn't have sniffed the top 25 two weeks ago.

Terrence Brown, North Carolina: Heading into the season, the assumption was that either Neo Avdalas or Matt Able would be UNC's top transfer, but this new addition from Utah has scored at least 14 points in each game so far and may be the most important player on Michael Malone's roster.

Collin Chandler, BYU: You could throw Syracuse transfer Tyler Betsey and Michigan State transfer Jaxon Kohler on here, too, as those two and Chandler are each averaging north of a dozen points per game in the early going for BYU. Chandler has made multiple twos, threes and free throws in each game, though. That scoring versatility might make him the Cougars' most important asset on offense.

Wes Enis, Creighton: The greenest light in the entire country is in Omaha. Enis averaged nearly 10 three-point attempts per game last year at South Florida. He has fired up 38 already through three games with Creighton, albeit sinking just 31.6 percent of them. Could he reach Kyle Korver's program record of 129 makes in a season?

Delrecco Gillespie, Houston: Dedan Thomas Jr. is the transfer du jour in Houston and ranks comfortably in our top 10. But this former Kent State star is already playing a major role in the paint, too. It's hard to imagine he'll replicate last year's 17.7 PPG and 11.3 RPG stat line now that he'll face much stiffer competition, but Gillespie might be one of the biggest X-factors of this college basketball season.

Juke Harris, Tennessee: Everyone had Harris as a top-10 player in the portal. However, after scoring in double figures in every game last season for the Demon Deacons, he went for just seven and six in his first two games with the Volunteers. We're not hitting the panic button yet, but we also can't justify putting him in the top 25 at the moment.

Isaiah Johnson and David Punch, Texas: While the Longhorns predictably destroyed Chicago State, Gardner-Webb, and Grambling State by a combined margin of 129 points, neither of these Big 12 exports (who averaged a combined 31.0 PPG last season) has made all that much of an impact. That narrative could shift on Sunday, though, if either one goes off against Baylor.

Acaden Lewis, Miami: The Villanova transfer looked like an early candidate for No. 1 on this list after scoring 24 on opening night against Florida. Since then, though, Lewis has been a ghost with just seven points (in 62 minutes played) between the subsequent victories over Wagner and North Florida. Kudos for showing up in the most important game, but what a bizarre 180.

Kayden Mingo, Baylor: Younger brother Dylan is the freshman phenom, but Kayden is the Mingo who put up 55 points in Baylor's exhibition games against Florida and Illinois. He hasn't been that prolific in three regular-season games, but Sunday's showdown with Texas could be the breakout party for this former Penn State star.

Milan Momcilovic, Kentucky: It would be malpractice not to at least mention the perimeter specialist many viewed as the top player in the portal. But is it going to work at Kentucky? Between the blowout loss to Kansas and the close call against James Madison, he scored a combined total of 12 points. In the Champions Classic, it seemed like the Wildcats had no clue how to create good looks for him.

Jackson Shelstad, Louisville: He and Flory Bidunga made themselves a package deal for the Cardinals. Of the two, the big man has gotten off to a better start, but Shelstad is certainly enjoying Pat Kelsey's permanent green light on three-pointers.

Jeremiah Wilkinson, Arkansas: There's nothing he could have done to save the Razorbacks in that beatdown they took from Virginia, but it is already abundantly clear that Wilkinson is Arkansas' perimeter offense this season. Through two games, he is 7-for-13 from deep, while the rest of the team is 6-for-24.

Nos. 25-22: Anton Bonke, Sananda Fru, Stefan Vaaks and Adam Clark

Last Season (Charlotte) : 10.6 PPG, 8.3 RPG, 1.5 BPG, 1.0 APG

Bonke immediately got into foul trouble against Duke on Tuesday and played virtually no part in that signature victory. But Michigan State's 7'2" starting center had a combined 20 points and 20 rebounds in 33 minutes played across his first two games. The Spartans are always great on the glass, but they could be extra special in that regard with this mountainous presence in the paint.

Early Returns : 10.0 PPG, 10.0 RPG, 2.0 BPG, 2.0 APG, 1.0 SPG

Last Season (Louisville) : 9.0 PPG, 6.1 RPG, 1.4 BPG, 1.2 APG

After years of priding himself on being a guy who didn't need the portal, even Shaka Smart admitted defeat and secured a key transfer to address the fact that Marquette's frontcourt was a disaster in 2025-26. Though he only averaged 22.5 minutes per game, Fru ranked fifth in the ACC last season in both offensive rebounds (99) and blocks (50). With 10 offensive rebounds and four blocks through two games, he might lead the Big East in both departments this season.

Early Returns : 13.7 PPG, 4.0 RPG, 2.0 APG, 33.3% 3PT

Last Season (Providence) : 15.8 PPG, 3.2 APG, 2.5 RPG, 35.0% 3PT

Vaaks was masterful in his Illini debut, scoring 20 points on nine field-goal attempts with four assists and no turnovers. In two games since then, though, he is 2-for-14 from three-point range and 3-for-10 from the charity stripe with two dimes and seven giveaways. He could be the national sixth man of the year...if he can reharness his shooting stroke.

Early Returns : 17.7 PPG, 5.3 APG, 3.0 RPG, 1.3 SPG

Last Season (Seton Hall) : 12.7 PPG, 4.9 APG, 3.0 RPG, 2.0 SPG

The jury is still out on whether Ole Miss is going to be a tournament-caliber team, but the Rebels have themselves one heck of a point guard in Clark. He's not a perimeter threat, but he can drive and dish (and defend) with the best of them. Don't be surprised if he somewhat takes over the Maui Invitational.

Nos. 21-19: Nick Townsend, John Blackwell and Keyshawn Hall

21. Nick Townsend, Stanford Early Returns : 22.7 PPG, 7.3 RPG, 5.0 APG, 2.7 SPG, 1.0 BPG, 50.0% 3PT Last Season (Yale) : 16.3 PPG, 7.4 RPG, 4.3 APG, 1.1 SPG, 46.3% 3PT

Townsend spent four years at Yale before going to Stanford for a graduate degree. You have to assume he's one of the most intelligent college basketball transfers. But he's also pretty brilliant on the court, a triple-double threat who racked up 31 points, eight rebounds and six assists in his most recent game against Rice. The Cardinal might have a 20 PPG guy for a third straight year, following in the footsteps of Maxime Raynaud and Ebuka Okorie.

20. John Blackwell, Duke Early Returns : 11.7 PPG, 3.0 RPG, 1.0 APG, 33.3% 3PT Last Season (Wisconsin) : 19.1 PPG, 5.1 RPG, 2.3 APG, 38.9% 3PT

Blackwell was a complete non-factor in Duke's opening-night rout of Army, but he was one of the only Blue Devils who bothered to show up for the Champions Classic loss to Michigan State, scoring 17 in that one. He almost made 100 triples last year with the Badgers. It's already clear he'll be letting 'em fly from deep all season long.

19. Keyshawn Hall, St. John's Early Returns : 19.5 PPG, 6.5 RPG, 1.0 APG, 1.0 SPG, 33.3% 3PT Last Season (Auburn) : 19.3 PPG, 7.1 RPG, 2.6 APG, 37.9% 3PT

If nothing else, we know Hall is going to attempt a lot of free throws for the Johnnies. He ranked top 10 in the nation with 266 last season at Auburn, as well as top 10 in 2024-25 with 244 at UCF. Hall also averaged roughly 19 points, seven rebounds and 2.5 assists per game in each of those seasons. After playing in the NIT championship last year and the Crown championship the previous year, this should be the year that this "five schools in five years" super senior finally partakes in the Big Dance.

Nos. 18-16: Bryson Tiller, Markus Burton and Sebastian Rancik

18. Bryson Tiller, Missouri Early Returns : 15.7 PPG, 8.7 RPG, 2.0 BPG, 2.0 APG, 50.0% 3PT Last Season (Kansas) : 7.9 PPG, 6.1 RPG, 1.3 BPG, 1.0 APG, 26.9% 3PT

Though the Tigers lost, Tiller was everywhere in Missouri's showdown with Saint Louis, finishing with 26 points, nine rebounds and four blocks. Most notably, 15 of those points came from the perimeter. He shot 5-for-23 from distance over his final 22 games with the Jayhawks, but was 5-for-8 against the Billikens. If that's legitimately part of this 6'11" rim-protector's game now, he might be a first-team All-SEC player.

17. Markus Burton, Indiana Early Returns : 13.7 PPG, 4.3 APG, 2.3 RPG, 1.7 SPG, 66.7% 3PT Last Season (Notre Dame) : 18.5 PPG, 3.7 APG, 2.8 RPG, 1.6 SPG, 30.6% 3PT

Burton lasted just 10 games last year before suffering an ankle injury that required surgery. Prior to that, though, he was well on his way to a third consecutive season with at least 500 points. After going for 20 points, four assists and three steals in the close win over Syracuse on Monday, it's already looking like he will be the go-to guy in Indiana's crowded backcourt. Let's see what he can do against Arkansas and Kentucky next week.

16. Sebastian Rancik, Florida State Early Returns : 22.0 PPG, 4.0 RPG, 2.0 APG Last Season (Colorado) : 12.3 PPG, 5.6 RPG, 2.0 APG

Florida State hasn't been to the NCAA tournament since 2021, but Rancik could be the driving force behind ending that drought. The Slovakian stretch-4 went for 23 points as the 'Noles gave No. 1 Florida a run for its money on Tuesday night. He has attempted eight free throws in each game thus far, making 88 percent of them. This 6'11" forward is also averaging six three-point attempts per game.

Nos. 15-13: Money Williams, Flory Bidunga and Paulius Murauskas

15. Money Williams, Boston College Early Returns : 21.7 PPG, 6.3 RPG, 4.3 APG, 1.0 SPG, 30.8% 3PT Last Season (Montana) : 20.6 PPG, 4.7 APG, 4.3 RPG, 34.0% 3PT

First-year head coach Luke Murray is looking to get Boston College into the dance for the first time since 2009. From a roster built almost entirely out of the portal, Williams is clearly going to be the straw that stirs the drink. He finished with 35 points, nine rebounds and five assists in the Eagles' convincing victory over Massachusetts. Watching Williams and UCF's Dior Johnson square off on Thanksgiving is going to be one heck of a treat.

14. Flory Bidunga, Louisville Early Returns : 13.0 PPG, 8.0 RPG, 2.0 SPG, 1.0 BPG, 1.0 APG Last Season (Kansas) : 13.3 PPG, 9.0 RPG, 2.6 BPG, 1.5 APG

Most of the transfer rankings from the summer had Bidunga and Milan Momcilovic in the top two spots. While Bidunga hasn't made that big of a statistical impact at his new Adidas school, the Cardinals weren't exactly challenged by Chattanooga or Morehead State, going on a 33-0 run during one stretch against the latter. Sunday at Memphis should be the first real test of how heavily Louisville will lean on its primary big man.

13. Paulius Murauskas, Arizona State Early Returns : 25.3 PPG, 8.3 RPG, 2.7 APG, 1.3 SPG, 1.0 BPG Last Season (Saint Mary's) : 18.4 PPG, 7.6 RPG, 2.1 APG

After 25 seasons at Saint Mary's, Randy Bennett finally left for a major conference gig. To make the transition smoother, he brought his biggest star with him from the Gaels to the Sun Devils. Murauskas has been even better than usual thus far, scoring at least 21 points in each of his first three games in the desert. Though, if you're taking a "Wake me when Big 12 play begins and he has to face some real competition" stance, point taken.

Nos. 12-10: Jaylen Petty, Baye Ndongo and Trey Kaufman-Renn

12. Jaylen Petty, UCLA Early Returns : 17.0 PPG, 5.5 RPG, 5.0 APG, 1.0 SPG, 58.3% 3PT Last Season (Texas Tech) : 9.9 PPG, 3.9 RPG, 2.2 APG, 37.5% 3PT

On Valentine's Day last season, Petty had two points, one rebound and one assist before fouling out in Texas Tech's overtime upset of Arizona. In his UCLA debut, though, he went for 13, seven and seven, respectively, plus two steals in an upset of Arizona. That might end up being his season-high in assists, but it wouldn't be the least bit surprising if he leads the Bruins in scoring. At any rate, there's a good chance he joins Bryce Alford as just the second player in UCLA history with at least 90 made triples in a single season.

11. Baye Ndongo, Pittsburgh Early Returns : 16.0 PPG, 11.7 RPG, 1.7 APG, 1.3 SPG Last Season (Georgia Tech) : 11.8 PPG, 8.1 RPG, 2.4 APG, 1.0 BPG

Ndongo is no stranger to double-doubles. He had 24 of them over the past three seasons with the Ramblin' Wreck. In his second game with Pitt, he went for 23 points and 21 rebounds, leading the Panthers back from what was a 15-point deficit in the second half against Buffalo. If he's the second coming of DeJuan Blair (15.7 PPG, 12.3 RPG in 2008-09), Pitt is going to be more of a factor than most were expecting.

10. Trey Kaufman-Renn, Kansas Early Returns : 12.7 PPG, 5.0 RPG, 3.3 APG Last Season (Purdue) : 14.2 PPG, 8.3 RPG, 2.5 APG

TKR is probably No. 1 on the "How in the world is that guy still playing college basketball?!" list of national outrage, added to Kansas' roster in mid-October and already playing a big role for one of the early title contenders. In Tuesday night's destruction of Kentucky, Kaufman-Renn finished with 12 points, six rebounds, six assists and two steals. He's also 2-for-2 from distance after going 2-for-13 last season.

Nos. 9-7: Donovan Dent, Jaland Lowe and Tre Singleton

Early Returns : 13.7 PPG, 8.3 APG, 3.3 SPG, 2.3 BPG, 1.7 RPG

Last Season (UCLA) : 13.3 PPG, 7.6 APG, 2.9 RPG, 1.7 SPG

Dent thought his playing career was over. He announced his retirement in May and returned to New Mexico to train young players rather than pursue professional basketball. Two months later, he reconsidered and applied for a fifth year of college eligibility. In this second installment of his final season, he went for 29 points, 20 assists and no turnovers in his first two games with LSU. The 6'2" point guard has also already blocked seven shots, compared to 12 in 35 games played last year. He has a huge game at Gonzaga on Saturday.

Early Returns : 18.3 PPG, 8.3 APG, 3.3 RPG, 55.6% 3PT

Last Season (Kentucky) : 8.0 PPG, 2.4 APG, 2.1 RPG, 20.8% 3PT

We never got a sustained look at what Lowe could do with Kentucky, as he dealt with shoulder injuries before the season even began. The lead guard who averaged 16.8 PPG and 5.5 APG at Pittsburgh two years ago appears to be back and better than ever. He went for 22 points and eight dimes in the statement win over Maryland. Then, he followed it up with 10 points and 15 assists in the subsequent way-too-close-for-comfort victory over Delaware State.

Early Returns : 19.3 PPG, 7.7 RPG, 1.7 APG, 1.3 BPG, 1.0 SPG

Last Season (Northwestern) : 7.6 PPG, 4.8 RPG, 1.5 APG

Singleton managed just one double-double as a freshman at Northwestern, but he has already emerged as a force in the paint for the Cyclones. He went for 11 points and 11 rebounds in his Iowa State debut against Memphis. He followed it up with 28, nine rebounds and three blocks in a comfortable win over Southern Miss. He's nowhere near the nightly triple-double threat that Joshua Jefferson was for this squad last year, but he could still be an All-American.

Nos. 6-4: Cruz Davis, PJ Haggerty and Tounde Yessoufou

6. Cruz Davis, Texas Tech Early Returns : 16.7 PPG, 5.3 RPG, 4.7 APG, 3.3 SPG Last Season (Hofstra) : 20.1 PPG, 4.7 APG, 3.7 RPG, 1.1 SPG

If Tuesday night's 20-point, five-assist gem against Illinois was your introduction to Cruz Davis, you missed out on two fun seasons of watching him cook at Hofstra. But now that the talent level of his supporting cast is much higher, things could be really fun this year. If JT Toppin eventually makes it back from his torn ACL, even better for Davis and the Red Raiders.

5. PJ Haggerty, Texas A&M Early Returns : 18.0 PPG, 3.3 RPG, 2.0 APG, 1.3 SPG, 57.1% 3PT Last Season (Kansas State) : 23.4 PPG, 5.3 RPG, 3.8 APG

Haggerty ranked fourth in the nation in scoring average last season, ranked third the previous year with Memphis and narrowly missed the top 10 in 2023-24 with Tulsa. All told, he averaged 22.1 points and 3.8 assists per game over the past three seasons, so it's little surprise that he has hit the ground running as the lead guard of the breakneck-paced Buckyball offense. He'll be in the spotlight Thursday night when the Aggies take on Oklahoma State in what is easily the most intriguing game of the day.

4. Tounde Yessoufou, St. John's Early Returns : 17.5 PPG, 6.0 RPG, 2.5 SPG, 1.5 APG, 1.5 BPG, 45.5% 3PT Last Season (Baylor) : 17.8 PPG, 5.9 RPG, 2.0 SPG, 1.6 APG, 29.3% 3PT

Yessoufou likely would have been a late first-round pick if he had chosen the one-and-done career path, but he opted for one more year of college ball—perhaps largely to show that he is a more reliable perimeter shooter than the sub-30 percent mark from his freshman season. To that end, so far, so good. He shot 4-for-7 from deep while stuffing the stat sheet in the Red Storm's blowout of Iona on Sunday. If that continues, he may well be the MVP of the Players Era 16 tournament during Feast Week.

Nos. 3-1: Dedan Thomas Jr., Jayden Reid and Dior Johnson

3. Dedan Thomas Jr., Houston Early Returns : 18.0 PPG, 6.5 APG, 2.5 RPG, 2.0 SPG, 66.7% 3PT Last Season (LSU) : 15.3 PPG, 6.5 APG, 2.7 RPG, 30.2% 3PT

From Marcus Sasser and Jamal Shead to LJ Cryer and Kingston Flemings, it's almost an annual tradition now for a Houston guard to make the 10-man Wooden All-American team. Thomas might be next. A foot injury prematurely ended his 2025-26 campaign; however, he has looked no worse for wear as the new driving force of the Cougars' offense. La Salle and California weren't exactly championship-caliber foes, but Thomas went for 13 assists and four steals with just one turnover in those first two games.

2. Jayden Reid, Memphis Early Returns : 23.0 PPG, 3.3 APG, 1.7 SPG, 46.2% 3PT Last Season (Northwestern) : 10.1 PPG, 5.0 APG, 1.0 SPG

Whether he'll be an All-American at the end of the year is questionable at best, but Reid was unofficially college basketball's MVP in the first week of the regular season. He almost single-handedly willed the Tigers to victories against Iowa State and VCU, scoring their final 11 points in the former and hitting the lead-flipping free throws in the closing seconds of the latter. (There was nothing he could do to save them at Vanderbilt, though.)

1. Dior Johnson, UCF Early Returns : 31.0 PPG, 4.3 APG, 3.0 RPG, 2.3 SPG, 58.8% 3PT Last Season (Tarleton State) : 24.0 PPG, 3.3 RPG, 1.6 APG, 1.2 SPG, 53.8% 3PT

Johnson played minimally for UCF two seasons ago before becoming a foul-drawing, scoring machine at Tarleton State in 2025-26. He has returned to the Knights in some sort of superhero cape. He went for 41 in the season-opening, overtime victory over Florida Gulf Coast before dropping 28 and 24, respectively, against Yale and South Alabama. We'll find out next week how his game translates to better competition, but he did put up 42 against Baylor last season. He's a must-watch every night.

articles.title: Knicks HC Calls Out Refs After Jalen Brunson Gets 0 FTs vs. Cavs, Star Deserves 'Better Whistle'
articles.summary: New York Knicks head coach Mike Brown was unhappy with the officiating, particularly pertaining to Jalen Brunson, in his team's 115-107 loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers on Wednesday.
articles.body:
New York Knicks head coach Mike Brown was unhappy with the officiating, particularly pertaining to Jalen Brunson, in his team's 115-107 loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers on Wednesday.

During his postgame press conference, Brown called Brunson having no free-throw attempts "pretty alarming" and that he would hope to "get a better whistle" from the officials.

"I just control what I can control and keep it at that," Brunson said when asked about not getting to the free-throw line.

Brunson still finished with a team-high 27 points in the loss. This was the first time he has played at least 35 minutes without attempting a free throw since Dec. 27, 2025, against the Atlanta Hawks.

The Cavaliers did have a 25-11 advantage in free-throw attempts. OG Anunoby and Karl-Anthony Towns were the only Knicks players who got to the line. Brunson is tied for 14th among all players with 7.1 free-throw attempts per game this season.

New York's 11 total free-throw attempts were its fewest in a game this season. The Knicks have only taken fewer than 20 free throws three times in 11 games so far in the 2026-27 campaign.

The Knicks' second-fewest free-throw attempts in a game this season is 14. It was done twice, most recently on Nov. 7 also against Cleveland.

Wednesday's loss snapped New York's four-game winning streak overall and five-game winning streak against the Cavs dating back to the Eastern Conference Finals last season.

Brunson and the Knicks will look to get back on track on Friday as they start a four-game road trip at Gainbridge Fieldhouse against the Indiana Pacers.

articles.title: “You make me feel like the luckiest girl”: Stephen Curry’s wife Ayesha Curry gets emotional with a heartfelt message as the NBA star stands up for her amid backlash
